content.title: About
content.content: Animal fat or drippings is the rendered fat obtained by slowly melting the fatty tissue of animals (commonly pork, beef or poultry). It is used in cooking as a source of saturated fat that adds flavor and richness to dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Historically animal fat was the main cooking medium before the widespread use of vegetable oils.
Different cultures have distinct names: "lard" in English, "salo" in Russian, "graisse" in French.
When stored properly, rendered fat can last for months, but it will eventually oxidize and lose its aroma.
In some cuisines, such as Mexican, animal fat is a key ingredient in traditional sauces like mole.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Animal fat provides about 9 kcal per gram, making it a concentrated source of energy.

items.title: Vitamins A and D
items.content: Rendered fat contains fat‑soluble vitamins, especially vitamin A and small amounts of vitamin D.

items.title: Improves absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients
items.content: The fat enhances the uptake of vitamins E, K and carotenoids from vegetables and fruits.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake of saturated fats may raise cholesterol levels and increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Oxidation and rancidity
items.content: When stored for long periods the fat can oxidize, forming harmful compounds; use fresh product.

items.title: Allergy to animal proteins
items.content: Some individuals may react to trace proteins remaining in the fat.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Animal fat is suitable for frying, roasting and braising, giving foods a golden crust and deep flavor. It can be used in baking (e.g., traditional pies), for sauces, and as a base for rich stocks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the fat in an airtight container in the refrigerator or a cool, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the freezer. Before use, check for a rancid smell – if present, discard the fat.

baby-toddler-fruit-and-vegetables-stage-.title: Baby Toddler fruit and vegetables, Stage 2

content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler fruit and vegetables, Stage 2 (4117) is a ready‑to‑serve puree blend of fruits and vegetables designed for infants aged 6–12 months. The purees are made from 100 % natural ingredients with no added sugar, salt or preservatives and meet pediatric nutrition guidelines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ingredients are sourced from certified growers who use pesticide‑free farming practices.
Each pack contains four 100 g servings that can be quickly heated in a microwave.
The product has been tested to be free of common allergens, except those listed in the label.
Purees have a smooth texture that supports the development of chewing skills in babies.
Packaging is recyclable and features a snap‑lock seal for easy opening.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The fruit and vegetable blend provides vitamin B6 and folate, which are important for nervous system development.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Dietary fiber for digestion
items.content: A modest amount of fiber helps regulate bowel movements in infants.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: No added salt aligns with recommendations to limit sodium in infant diets.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients from the fruits and vegetables protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although the product contains no typical allergens, parents of children with known food allergies should review the ingredient list.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the container refrigerated and use within 24 hours.

items.title: Heating temperature
items.content: Overheating can degrade some vitamins; heat to body temperature (≈ 37 °C) before serving.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat a serving in the microwave for 30–40 seconds, stir, and let it cool to a comfortable temperature. The puree can be served alone or mixed with infant cereal, yogurt, or breast milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packs in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the container sealed in the refrigerator and consume within a day.

beef-potatoes-and-vegetables-excluding-c.title: Beef, potatoes and vegetables without carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens; cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender beef, boiled potatoes and a mix of vegetables (such as cauliflower, bell pepper and zucchini) prepared without carrots, broccoli or dark‑green leafy greens, served under a rich cheese sauce. This combination provides a balanced flavor, juicy meat and a creamy sauce texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of iron that is more readily absorbed than plant‑based forms.
Potatoes retain most of their vitamin C when steamed or baked in the skin.
Cheese sauce is often made from cheddar cheese and milk, giving the dish its characteristic golden hue.
Excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens makes the dish gentler on sensitive stomachs.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and some vegetables deliver vitamins B6 and B12, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, beneficial for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables like bell pepper and zucchini contain vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Cheese sauce can be rich in saturated fats, so people with high cholesterol should limit portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheeses often contain a lot of salt; those with hypertension should choose a low‑sodium version.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should replace the sauce with a plant‑based alternative.

items.title: Digestibility of beef
items.content: Heavy cuts of beef may be harder to digest for those with stomach issues; thinly sliced pieces are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, arranging beef, potatoes and vegetables on a plate and drizzling the cheese sauce over the top. Garnish with fresh parsley for aroma. Pair with whole‑grain bread or a light salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 2 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or broth to keep the sauce from becoming too thick. Freezing is not recommended because the cheese texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean beef, boiled rice and a mix of vegetables (such as bell pepper, zucchini, peas), without carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens or sauces. It is a balanced meal rich in protein and complex carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is one of the richest sources of iron and zinc.
Rice is a staple energy source in many cultures, especially in Asia.
The absence of sauce makes the dish low‑calorie and lets the natural flavors shine.
Traditionally beef is seared on high heat to lock in juices and retain tenderness.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice releases glucose slowly, helping maintain stable energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beef and rice contain B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meal supplies iron, zinc and magnesium, supporting immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Without sauces or sweet vegetables, the dish is suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Red meat consumption
items.content: Excessive intake of red meat may be linked to higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: If soy sauce is used, consider possible gluten allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Watch added salt during cooking to stay within daily sodium recommendations.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot; fresh herbs such as parsley or dill can be added for extra flavor. It works as a standalone lunch or as part of a larger menu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly until boiling to eliminate any bacteria.

bitter-melon-horseradish-jute-or-radish-.title: Bitter melon, horseradish, jute, or radish leaves, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Bitter melon (Momordica charantia), horseradish (Armoracia rusticana), jute leaves (Corchorus capsularis) and radish leaves (Raphanus sativus) are edible plant parts that are commonly cooked to soften their texture and mellow their sharp flavors while retaining nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bitter melon is a staple in Asian cuisines and traditional medicine.
Horseradish root contains glucosinolates that convert to pungent allyl isothiocyanate when grated.
Jute leaves are high in fiber and are used in many Southeast Asian dishes.
Radish leaves grow quickly and can be harvested within 3–4 weeks of sowing.
All four vegetables are rich sources of B‑vitamins and vitamin C.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and antioxidants in these vegetables help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Bitter melon is known for its glucose‑lowering properties, useful for pre‑diabetic individuals.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effects
items.content: Glucosinolates from horseradish and polyphenols in jute leaves have anti‑inflammatory activity.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Fiber from radish and jute leaves promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Liver detoxification
items.content: Certain compounds in bitter melon support the liver’s ability to clear toxins.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Large amounts of horseradish or bitter melon may cause heartburn or gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to horseradish or radish leaves.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Bitter melon can potentiate the effect of hypoglycemic medications.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Radish leaves contain oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Toxicity of unripe bitter melon
items.content: Unripe fruit contains carbolic acid, which is toxic in high doses.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The vegetables can be boiled, stewed, baked, or quickly stir‑fried. Bitter melon is often diced and added to soups; horseradish is grated into sauces; jute and radish leaves are used in salads, curries, or as fillings for pancakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Cooked dishes should be stored in airtight containers and consumed within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal raisin cookie is a soft‑to‑chewy biscuit made from whole oat flakes, wheat flour, butter, sugar and dried raisins. It offers a gentle sweet flavor with a hint of caramelized raisin and a characteristic oat aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are considered one of the most nutritious grains and are a staple in wholesome diets.
Raisins retain some of their antioxidant properties even after baking.
Adding raisins to baked goods dates back to medieval recipes where dried fruit served as a natural sweetener.
Oatmeal cookies are often viewed as a healthier alternative to classic sugar cookies because of their higher fiber content.
In some regions the cookie is referred to as “muesli cookie.”

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole oat flakes provide soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver steady energy without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Raisins are a good source of iron, while oats supply magnesium, both essential for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in raisins help combat free radicals.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Beta‑glucans from oats may help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The cookie contains added sugar and raisins, so people monitoring glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour is used in the recipe, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, the cookie is relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt or ice cream, or use it as a base for dessert parfaits. It pairs well with tea, coffee, or milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness. Discard any cookies that become soggy or develop mold.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-an.title: Egg Omelet with Meat and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled eggs with added meat and tomatoes is a nutritious dish often enjoyed for breakfast or a light dinner. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, meat adds extra iron and B‑vitamins, and tomatoes contribute fresh flavor and lycopene.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that enhances cellular protection.
Combining eggs with meat increases the bioavailability of iron compared to eating them separately.
Omelets are easily adapted to dietary needs: lean cuts of meat or turkey can be used instead of fattier options.
The tradition of adding fillings to omelets exists worldwide—from French "omelette aux fines herbes" to Mexican "huevos revueltos con chorizo".

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat together supply all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 from meat and eggs support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, which may help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin D from eggs and zinc from meat contribute to a healthy immune response.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The blend of protein and moderate fat delivers lasting satiety and steady energy.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Meat can be a source of saturated fat; choose lean cuts or limit the portion size.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to eggs and should avoid this dish.

items.title: Cholesterol levels
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to prevent salmonella and other bacterial risks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in diced cooked or lean meat and chopped tomatoes, then cook in a lightly oiled pan until set to your liking. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-to.title: Egg Omelet with Meat, Tomatoes, and Dark-Green Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet enriched with lean meat, fresh tomatoes, and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale) is a nutrient‑dense dish high in protein, vitamins, and minerals. Cooked with a small amount of oil, it makes a balanced breakfast or light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable complete protein sources.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables contain chlorophyll, which supports body detoxification.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that promotes heart health.
Lean meats such as turkey or chicken breast add iron and zinc without excess saturated fat.
The omelet can be easily customized by swapping different meats and vegetables.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B2, B6, and B12 vitamins aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from green vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C in tomatoes and vitamin A in green vegetables boost immune defenses.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared with minimal oil, the dish remains heart‑friendly.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: Processed meat concerns
items.content: Choose lean, minimally processed cuts to avoid excess sodium and additives.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While eggs are nutritious, people with high cholesterol should moderate intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk, stir in diced meat, chopped tomatoes, and green vegetables. Cook in a skillet with a little olive oil, stirring gently until set. Garnish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Ham and noodles, no sauce is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled egg noodles, sliced cooked ham, and a pinch of seasoning. It contains no tomato or cream sauces, making it suitable for those avoiding extra fats and sugars.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is commonly served in school and office cafeterias as a quick lunch.
The noodles are usually cooked "al dente" to retain a pleasant bite.
The ham used is typically smoked, giving the dish its characteristic aroma.
Lack of sauce reduces the calorie count compared with similar sauced versions.
Ham and noodles, no sauce often appear in travel‑friendly "instant meals" packs.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham is a good source of vitamin B12 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles
items.content: Noodles deliver a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Absence of sauce means the dish contains minimal added sugars.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed ham often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some hams are cured with nitrites, which may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat noodles contain gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Ham contains saturated fats that should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish is ready to eat after reheating in a microwave or on the stove. It can be served as a standalone meal or paired with fresh vegetables or herbs for added flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package refrigerated at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑4 days. When frozen, the dish retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: The Whole Wheat Raisin Muffin is a baked good made from whole‑grain wheat flour and naturally sweetened with raisins. It has a soft, slightly moist crumb, warm spice aromas, and a sweet raisin finish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain flour retains bran and germ, making the muffin more nutritious than those made with white flour.
Raisins add natural sweetness as well as small amounts of iron and potassium.
Traditional muffin recipes include leavening agents to achieve a light texture.
Muffins are often served with tea or coffee as a quick snack.
When stored properly, a whole‑wheat muffin keeps its spice aroma for up to a week.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour and raisins provide dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Raisins are high in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar stability
items.content: Fiber slows glucose absorption, contributing to more stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates from whole‑grain flour give lasting satiety and energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins add natural sugars; those monitoring sugar intake should account for it.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Muffins can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Dried fruit sensitivity
items.content: Raisins may cause digestive discomfort in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a standalone snack, split and topped with cottage cheese, added to yogurt, or used as a base for sweet sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or refrigerate for up to a week. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-and-added-.title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce and Added Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with a tomato-based sauce and added vegetables is a dish of cooked noodles topped with a sauce made from ripe tomatoes and mixed vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini, carrot, and broccoli. The sauce gives the dish a bright flavor, while the vegetables add texture and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce has been a staple of Italian cuisine for over a thousand years.
Adding vegetables to pasta increases the content of vitamins A, C, and K as well as dietary fiber.
Pasta made from durum wheat (semolina) has a lower glycemic index than soft‑wheat pasta.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives the sauce its vivid red color.
Quick sautéing of vegetables before adding them to the sauce preserves their crunch and nutrients.

items.title: Rich source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy through slow‑release glucose, helping to keep you full longer.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables supply vitamin C, vitamin A and lycopene, supporting immune function and protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain pasta boost fiber content, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The dish is typically prepared with minimal oil, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables provide potassium, magnesium and iron, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared tomato sauces often contain added salt; monitor sodium levels when cooking.

items.title: Acidity of tomatoes
items.content: Individuals with gastritis or reflux may experience discomfort from the acidic sauce.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some commercial sauces may include preservatives or sweeteners that are not suitable for all diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and vegetables. A drizzle of olive oil, grated Parmesan, or fresh herbs (basil, oregano) can enhance flavor. It works as a standalone meal or as part of a larger menu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. When frozen, the dish keeps up to 2 months after cooling and sealing in a freezer‑safe bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Grilled scallops are tender marine mollusks from the Pectinidae family. They have a mildly sweet, slightly nutty flavor and a firm yet delicate texture. Grilling enhances their natural aroma, making them a favorite in both restaurant and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scallops can “swim” by rapidly clapping their shells together.
There are two main types: large sea scallops and smaller bay scallops.
Scallops can open and close their shells in fractions of a second to evade predators.
In Japan, scallops are often served raw as sashimi, while Western cuisines favor grilling or pan‑searing.
The harvest season is typically fall and winter, when the meat is most firm.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Grilled scallops provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 1 g of fat per 100 g, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Scallops are a good source of zinc, magnesium, and selenium, which support immunity and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of EPA and DHA contribute to heart and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Scallops can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Proper handling
items.content: Improperly stored or expired scallops can cause foodborne illness; always check for off‑odors and texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled scallops can be served as a main dish, tossed in salads, mixed into pasta, or placed atop rice dishes. A squeeze of lemon, drizzle of olive oil, and fresh herbs enhance their flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked scallops in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a sealed bag, where they retain quality for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Sour cream light is a low‑fat dairy product made by fermenting skimmed milk with starter cultures. It has a smooth, creamy texture, a mild tangy flavor, and contains about 5 % fat, making it a lighter alternative to regular sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light sour cream is often used in sauces, dressings, and desserts where reduced calories are desired.
Unlike full‑fat versions, light sour cream may contain stabilizers to maintain its creamy consistency at low fat levels.
Traditionally, sour cream originates from Eastern European cuisines and is a staple in many regional dishes.
Many brands fortify light sour cream with vitamin D and calcium to boost its nutritional profile.
When stored properly (refrigerated at +2‑+4 °C) it stays fresh for up to 10 days after opening.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Contains roughly 5 % fat, allowing you to lower the overall calorie count of dishes without sacrificing creaminess.

items.title: Rich in Calcium
items.content: Provides about 10 % of the daily calcium requirement per 100 g serving, supporting bone health.

items.title: Probiotic Cultures
items.content: Fermentation creates live bacteria that can help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Vitamin B12
items.content: Supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Does not cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, suitable for glycemic control.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose; individuals with intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: May trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to casein.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Some brands add stabilizers or preservatives; check the label if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use light sour cream in sauces, dips, casseroles, as a salad dressing, in baking, and in desserts. It pairs well with berries, fruits, and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at +2‑+4 °C in the original container. After opening, keep tightly sealed. Use within 7‑10 days. Do not freeze.
